resources.string: LuxRamp watches the room with its own light sensor loop, so the screen moves when the light does instead of catching up ten seconds later.
Everything LuxRamp needs, asked for once, here.
Still waiting on %1$s. Grant it there, or stop the run.
Everything required is granted. LuxRamp is ready to run.
Continue unlocks once the required items are granted. Skipping is fine too: LuxRamp will run in a reduced form and you can grant the rest later in Settings.
Lets LuxRamp save the brightness it settles on, so the system slider agrees with the screen, and notice when you move that slider yourself.
Android will not run a background service without one. You can hide the notification again under HyperOS extras, and the service keeps going.
HyperOS freezes the service once the screen goes off unless LuxRamp is unrestricted, and the ramp freezes with it.
The reason LuxRamp is fast: with Shizuku it writes brightness straight to the display. Without it the system performs the ramp, which is the slow behaviour this app exists to replace.
Only for the floating panel: a small window that stays on top with brightness, an off switch and the ramp offset.
Not installed. Install Shizuku, or Sui on a rooted device, then come back.
Installed but not running. Start it from the Shizuku app.
Running. It only needs your authorisation for LuxRamp.
Authorised. Brightness writes go straight to the display.
Follow the device, or pin LuxRamp to light or dark whatever the system is doing.
Take the colours from your wallpaper. Turn it off to choose one of the palettes instead.
Each swatch previews that theme with its own background and its own three accents, in the mode you are in right now.
A small window that stays on top of other apps, with a brightness slider, a switch that turns automatic control off, and the ramp offset.
Needs permission to display over other apps. Grant it, then switch this on.
The panel dims itself once you stop touching it, so it stops competing with whatever is underneath.
How long the panel stays fully visible after the last touch.
How visible the panel stays once it has faded. Lower keeps it out of the way, and makes it harder to find again.
How far the light has to move before LuxRamp reacts. Higher leaves the screen alone through small wobbles in the room, like a page turning under a lamp.
Two vendor switches that cannot be read back, so neither will ever tick itself off. LuxRamp can only open them for you.
Allow LuxRamp in the Security app so it comes back after a reboot.
Turns the service notification channel off. The service keeps running, only the notification goes away.
LuxRamp reads the ambient light sensor itself and drives the panel with a ramp you can see and tune, instead of the fixed, slow one the system runs.
